newsitem.title: INDIA: India's populous Uttar Pradesh, political keystone.
newsitem.headline: India's populous Uttar Pradesh, political keystone.

text.p: India's most populous state, Uttar Pradesh, is a showcase for the shifting alliances and caste-based parties that have transformed national politics.
Nine of India's 12 prime ministers have come from the sprawling state which is bisected by the mighty Ganges river and has 140 million people -- more than Japan or Pakistan.
Most of the prime ministers from the state were from the Congress party, which has ruled India for all but four years since independence in 1947.
But Congress has fallen on hard times in Uttar Pradesh, losing clout there as it has through much of the world's second most populous nation, behind China.

Drawing the bulk of its support from the northern Hindi-speaking belt which includes Uttar Pradesh, the right-wing Hindu Bharatiya Janata Party (BJP) has used the volatile state and religious issues as a springboard to national prominence.
Uttar Pradesh, with some 100 million eligible voters, sends 85 deputies to the 545-member lower house of the federal parliament in New Delhi, far more than any other state.
In general elections ended last May, the BJP captured 52 seats from Uttar Pradesh. Congress took five.
Little wonder that the BJP hopes a strong showing in the Uttar Pradesh polls will cripple Prime Minister H.D. Deve Gowda's centre-left coalition in Delhi and force mid-term general elections.
While most opinion surveys show the BJP emerging as the front-runner in the assembly polls, the party which claims India has a single Hindu culture was not assured of winning an outright majority.

The BJP ruled the state in December 1992, when Hindu fanatics tore down a 16th century mosque in Ayodhya, 200 km (120 miles) east of the state capital Lucknow. The destruction of the mosque triggered Hindu-Moslem riots in which more than 3,000 people were killed across the country.
In the resulting confusion, the BJP government was dismissed and the state put under direct federal rule.
The BJP won 176 of 425 seats in the Uttar Pradesh state assembly in the last local polls in 1993.

But an alliance between two regional parties -- the Bahujan Samaj Party (BSP) representing low-caste Hindus, and the Samajwadi Party (SP) representing minorities and backward castes -- managed to clinch power.
Eighteen months later, BSP chief Kanshi Ram struck a deal with the BJP, provoking the fall of the coalition government headed by SP leader Mulayam Singh Yadav.
BSP member Mayawati (one name) became the first low-caste woman to be a chief minister when she was installed at the head of a government backed by the BJP in June 1995.
But as the alliance was one of sheer political convenience between longstanding antagonists, it lasted only four months, falling in October 1995. Direct federal rule ensued.

In this year's polls, the BSP has allied with Congress. In a reflection of the shift towards caste-based, regional politics, the BSP candidates are contesting 229 constituencies and Congress only 126.
